title: Grade XII Physics Model Question 2082 (Set 1)
description: A full NEB-pattern Grade XII physics model paper (Groups A, B and C) with worked solutions for every question.

groups.title: Group A
groups.subtitle: Multiple choice questions

questions.q: If a gymnast on a rotating stool with his arms outstretched suddenly lowers his arms,
questions.solution: Explanation: When the gymnast lowers his arms, the mass distribution moves closer to the axis of rotation. This reduces the moment of inertia (I = Σmr²). Since no external torque acts, angular momentum L = Iω is conserved. As I decreases, ω increases.

questions.q: The motion of a particle executing simple harmonic motion is given by x = 0.01 sin 100π(t + 0.05), where x is in meters and t in second. The time period in second is
questions.solution:
Solution: Comparing with x = A sin(ωt + φ), we get ω = 100π rad/s.

T = 2π/ω = 2π/(100π) = 2/100 = 0.02 s

questions.q: What fraction of a wooden raft of density 0.8 g/cc will be outside the sea water of density 1.2 g/cc?
questions.solution:
Solution: By law of floatation:

ρraft × V × g = ρwater × Vsub × g
Vsub/V = ρraft/ρwater = 0.8/1.2 = 2/3

Fraction outside = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3

questions.q: In figure, how much work is done by the system in process AB?
questions.solution:
Solution: Work done = Area under P-V curve (trapezium AB)

PA = 2.6 × 10&sup6; N/m², PB = 2.0 × 10&sup6; N/m²
VA = 1.0 × 10−3 m³, VB = 4.0 × 10−3 m³

W = ½(PA + PB) × (VB − VA)
W = ½(2.6 + 2.0) × 10&sup6; × (4.0 − 1.0) × 10−3
W = 6.9 × 10³ J

questions.q: The diagram shows the pressure volume relationship for a fixed mass of an ideal gas that undergoes a cycle XYZ. In which part(s) of the cycle is external work done on the gas?
options: Y → Z and Z → X only
X → Y and Z → X only
questions.solution:
Explanation: External work is done ON the gas when the gas is compressed (volume decreases).

  • X → Y: Volume decreases (compression) → Work done on gas ✓
  • Y → Z: Volume constant (isochoric) → No work done
  • Z → X: Volume increases (expansion) → Work done by gas

questions.q: The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator working between the ice point (0°C) and room temperature 27°C is
questions.solution:
Tcold = 0°C = 273 K
Thot = 27°C = 300 K

COP = Tcold / (Thot − Tcold)
COP = 273 / (300 − 273) = 273 / 27 ≈ 10

questions.q: A diffraction pattern is obtained using a beam of red light. What will be the effect on the diffraction pattern if the red light is replaced by white light?
options: All bright fringes except central one, becomes white.
All bright fringes except central one, becomes colorful.
questions.solution: The central maximum contains all wavelengths superimposed, so it appears white. Higher-order fringes spread into spectra because fringe position y = nλD/d depends on wavelength. Each order becomes a rainbow (colorful), with red farthest from center and violet closest.

questions.q: The sound levels of two waves of same frequency in a given medium are 100 dB and 20 dB respectively. How many times is the intensity I<sub>1</sub> greater than I<sub>2</sub>?
questions.solution:
β1 − β2 = 10 log(I1/I2)
100 − 20 = 10 log(I1/I2)
80 = 10 log(I1/I2)
log(I1/I2) = 8
I1/I2 = 108

questions.q: If the emf of a thermocouple, one junction of which is kept at 0°C, is given by E = aθ + ½bθ², where a and b are constants, then the neutral temperature will be
questions.solution:
Neutral temperature is where emf is maximum (dE/dθ = 0).

E = aθ + ½bθ²
dE/dθ = a + bθ = 0
θn = −a/b

questions.q: The value of magnetizing field (H) when the magnetic flux density (B) is equal to zero, is called
questions.solution: Coercivity is the reverse magnetizing field H required to reduce B to zero after magnetization. Retentivity is the value of B when H = 0.

questions.q: What is the point where the seismic waves start, called?
questions.solution: The hypocenter (or focus) is the point within the Earth where an earthquake rupture starts. The epicenter is the point directly above it on the Earth's surface.

groups.title: Group B
groups.subtitle: Short answer questions

parts.q: Define torque. Derive a relation between torque and moment of inertia.
parts.solution:
Torque: The turning effect of a force about an axis: τ = F × r.

Derivation: For a particle of mass mi at distance ri:

Fi = miriα
τi = Firi = miri²α
Total τ = Σmiri²α = Iα
τ = Iα

parts.q: Calculate the radius of gyration of a uniform rod of mass 20 kg and length 30 cm about an axis passing through one end and perpendicular to its length.
parts.solution:
I = ML²/3 = 20 × (0.30)²/3 = 0.6 kg m²
K = √(I/M) = √(0.6/20) = √0.03
K = 0.173 m = 17.3 cm

parts.q: State and explain the principle of conservation of angular momentum.
parts.solution:
Principle: If no external torque acts, total angular momentum remains constant: Iω = constant.

When a spinning person pulls their arms in, I decreases and ω increases proportionally. This explains divers tucking to spin faster.

parts.q: Explain why a water drop sticks on glass but mercury does not.
parts.solution:
Water: Adhesive force (water-glass) > Cohesive force. Water spreads and sticks (wetting).

Mercury: Cohesive force > Adhesive force. Mercury forms droplets and does not stick (non-wetting).

parts.q: Derive and explain the equation of continuity.
parts.solution:
Mass flow rate is constant:
ρA1v1 = ρA2v2

For incompressible fluid:
A1v1 = A2v2 = constant

Where the tube is narrow, fluid flows faster.

parts.q: Terminal velocity of a glass ball in glycerin. Densities: glass 2.6 g/cc, glycerin 1.32 g/cc. Viscosity 0.8 poise. Radius 2 mm.
parts.solution:
v = (2/9) × r²(ρ − σ)g / η
v = (2/9) × (0.2)² × (2.6 − 1.32) × 980 / 0.8
v = 13.94 cm/s ≈ 0.14 m/s

parts.q: What is simple harmonic motion?
parts.solution: SHM is periodic motion where restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and directed toward the mean position: F = −kx.

parts.q: Show that velocity in SHM is maximum at mean position and minimum at extreme.
parts.solution:
v = ω√(A² − x²)

At mean (x = 0): vmax = Aω
At extreme (x = A): vmin = 0

parts.q: Chair (42.5 kg) oscillates with period 1.30 s empty and 2.45 s with a person. Find the person's mass.
State first law of thermodynamics and derive Mayer's relation C<sub>p</sub> − C<sub>v</sub> = R.
parts.solution:
First Law: dQ = dU + dW = dU + PdV

At constant volume: dQ = CvdT = dU

At constant pressure: dQ = CpdT = dU + PdV = CvdT + RdT

Cp − Cv = R

parts.q: Compare efficiency of petrol and diesel engines based on compression ratios.
parts.solution:
Petrol: r = 7–10, efficiency ≈ 25–30%

Diesel: r = 15–22, efficiency ≈ 35–45%

Higher compression ratio in diesel engines gives higher thermal efficiency.

parts.q: What is Doppler's effect?
parts.solution: Apparent change in frequency due to relative motion between source and observer.

parts.q: Derive apparent frequency when observer moves toward stationary source.
parts.solution:
f' = f(v + vo)/v

Relative velocity of sound increases, so observed frequency increases.

parts.q: Train at 40 km/h sounds whistle 580 Hz. Observer stationary. Speed of sound 1200 km/h. Find observed frequency.
parts.solution:
f' = f × v/(v − vs)
f' = 580 × 1200/(1200 − 40)
f' = 580 × 1200/1160
f' = 600 Hz

parts.q: Define harmonics and overtone.
parts.solution:
Harmonics: Integral multiples of fundamental frequency (f, 2f, 3f...).

Overtones: Frequencies higher than fundamental actually present in a note.

parts.q: Condition for equal fundamental frequencies of closed and open pipe.
parts.solution:
v/(4Lc) = v/(2Lo)
Lo = 2Lc

Open pipe length must be twice the closed pipe length.

parts.q: Wavelength at 25°C if f = 256 Hz and v<sub>0</sub> = 330 m/s.
parts.solution:
v25 = 330 × √(298/273) = 344.8 m/s
λ = v/f = 344.8/256
λ = 1.35 m

parts.q: Principle of potentiometer. Why is it called an ideal voltmeter?
parts.solution:
Principle: V ∝ L for a uniform wire.

Ideal voltmeter: At null point, no current is drawn from the cell being measured, so it gives true emf without loading error.

parts.q: Principles behind Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws.
parts.solution:
KCL: Conservation of charge.

KVL: Conservation of energy.

parts.q: Find current in 2Ω resistor using Kirchhoff's laws.
parts.solution:
Left loop: 35 = 5I1 + 2I2 ...(i)
Right loop: 20 = I1 + 3I2 ...(ii)
Solving: I1 = 5 A, I2 = 5 A
Current in 2Ω = I1 + I2 = 10 A

parts.q: Why does a magnetic field develop around a current-carrying conductor?
parts.solution: Moving charges (current) produce a magnetic field. Field lines form concentric circles around the wire; direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule.

parts.q: Use Biot-Savart law to find B at center of circular coil.
parts.solution:
dB = (μ0/4π) Idl/r²
Integrating: B = μ0NI/(2r)

parts.q: Circular coil: N=100, r=10 cm, I=5 A. Find B on axis at 5 cm from centre.
parts.solution:
B = μ0NIr²/[2(r²+x²)^(3/2)]
B = (4π×10−7×100×5×0.01)/[2(0.0125)^(3/2)]
B = 2.25 × 10−3 T = 2.25 mT

parts.q:
Energy levels of a hypothetical one-electron atom: En = −13.6/n² eV.
a) Compute four lowest energy levels and construct energy level diagram.
parts.solution:
E1 = −13.6/1² = −13.6 eV
E2 = −13.6/4 = −3.4 eV
E3 = −13.6/9 = −1.51 eV
E4 = −13.6/16 = −0.85 eV

Energy level diagram: n=1 at −13.6 eV (ground), n=2 at −3.4 eV, n=3 at −1.51 eV, n=4 at −0.85 eV, with spacing decreasing as n increases.

parts.q: What is the first excitation potential?
parts.solution:
First excitation potential = E2 − E1
= −3.4 − (−13.6) = 10.2 V

parts.q: Electrons accelerated through 16.2 V bombard ground-state atoms. What wavelengths are emitted?
parts.solution:
16.2 eV can excite atoms from n=1 to n=3 (E3 − E1 = 12.09 eV) or n=1 to n=4 (E4 − E1 = 12.75 eV), but not to n=∞ (13.6 eV).

λ = hc/ΔE = 1240 eV-nm / ΔE

3→1: λ = 1240/12.09 = 102.6 nm
3→2: λ = 1240/1.89 = 656 nm
2→1: λ = 1240/10.2 = 121.6 nm

parts.q: Which property of a semiconductor diode permits it to be used as a rectifier?
parts.solution: The unidirectional conductivity (allowing current in forward bias and blocking in reverse bias) of a p-n junction diode makes it suitable for rectification.

parts.q: Discuss p-n junction diode as a full-wave rectifier.
parts.solution:
A full-wave rectifier uses a centre-tapped transformer and two diodes (or four diodes in a bridge configuration).

During positive half-cycle, one diode conducts; during negative half-cycle, the other conducts. Both half-cycles are rectified, giving pulsating DC in the same direction. The output frequency is twice the input frequency.

groups.title: Group C
groups.subtitle: Long answer questions

parts.q: What is interference? Discuss the importance of coherent sources.
parts.solution:
Interference: The superposition of two waves resulting in a pattern of alternating bright and dark regions (constructive and destructive interference).

Importance of coherent sources: Coherent sources maintain a constant phase difference, producing stable and observable interference patterns. Without coherence, the phase difference changes rapidly and the pattern averages out to uniform illumination.

parts.q: Show that width of bright fringe equals width of dark fringe in Young's double slit experiment.
parts.solution:
Position of nth bright fringe: ynbright = nλD/d

Position of nth dark fringe: yndark = (2n−1)λD/(2d)

Fringe width (bright) = yn+1b − ynb = λD/d
Fringe width (dark) = yn+1d − ynd = λD/d

Both fringe widths are equal: β = λD/d

parts.q: Why is a diffraction grating better than double slit for measuring wavelength?
parts.solution: A diffraction grating produces sharper, brighter, and widely separated maxima. The angular separation is large and measurable accurately, whereas double-slit fringes are broad and less distinct.

parts.q: Unpolarized light incident at 55° on glass. Reflected beam is completely polarized. Find refractive index and angle of refraction.
parts.solution:
By Brewster's law: μ = tan(ip)

μ = tan(55°) = 1.428

Also, μ = sin(ip)/sin(r)
sin(r) = sin(55°)/1.428 = 0.819/1.428 = 0.574
r = 35.0°

(Note: ip + r = 90° at Brewster angle, so r = 35°)

parts.q: Define RMS value of alternating current.
parts.solution: The RMS (Root Mean Square) value of AC is the steady DC current that produces the same heating effect in a given resistor in a given time as the AC does. For sinusoidal current: Irms = I0/√2.

parts.q: Discuss LCR circuit with phasor diagram to find current and impedance.
parts.solution:
In an LCR series circuit, voltages across L and C are 180° out of phase. The net reactive voltage is VL − VC.

V = √[VR² + (VL − VC)²]
Impedance: Z = √[R² + (XL − XC)²]
where XL = ωL, XC = 1/(ωC)

Phase angle: tanφ = (XL − XC)/R
Current: I = V/Z

Phasor diagram: VR along x-axis, VL upward, VC downward. Resultant V is the vector sum.

parts.q: What is electrical resonance? Obtain expression for resonant frequency. Draw current vs frequency curve.
parts.solution:
Electrical resonance: The condition in an LCR circuit when XL = XC, making the circuit purely resistive and current maximum.

XL = XC
ω0L = 1/(ω0C)
ω0² = 1/(LC)
f0 = 1/(2π√LC)

Current vs frequency curve: Bell-shaped curve peaking at f0. Sharp peak for low resistance (high Q-factor), broad peak for high resistance.

parts.q: LCR circuit: R=25Ω, L=30 mH, C=10 µF, E<sub>rms</sub>=220 V, f=50 Hz. Find current.
State Lenz's law and explain demonstration with coil and magnet.
parts.solution:
Lenz's Law: The induced current always flows in a direction that opposes the change causing it.

Demonstration: When a bar magnet's N-pole is pushed toward a coil, induced current creates a N-pole on the near side of the coil, repelling the magnet. When pulled away, it creates a S-pole, attracting the magnet. This opposition requires work, converting mechanical energy to electrical energy.

parts.q: Vehicle brake with aluminium disc and electromagnets.
parts.solution:
i) How emf induction causes slowing: The rotating aluminium disc cuts through the magnetic field of the electromagnets, inducing eddy currents in the disc (Faraday's law). By Lenz's law, these currents create a magnetic field that opposes the motion of the disc, producing a braking torque that slows the vehicle.

ii) Why braking increases with speed: Faster rotation means the disc cuts more magnetic flux per second (greater dΦ/dt), inducing larger eddy currents. Since braking force is proportional to eddy current, higher speed produces stronger braking.

parts.q: Find emf in a conductor: l=20 cm, r=10 cm from axis, B=0.5 T, 1000 rpm.
parts.solution:
ω = 2πN/60 = 2π × 1000/60 = 104.7 rad/s
v = rω = 0.10 × 104.7 = 10.47 m/s

emf = Blv = 0.5 × 0.20 × 10.47
emf = 1.047 V ≈ 1.05 V

parts.q:
Carbon-14 has half-life 5760 years. Produced by: 147N + 10n → 146C + X
a) Define half-life and decay constant. Relation between them.
parts.solution:
Half-life (T1/2): Time for half the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay.

Decay constant (λ): Probability of decay per unit time.

T1/2 = ln(2)/λ = 0.693/λ

parts.q: Identify particle X.
parts.solution: Balancing mass and atomic numbers: X is a proton (11H or 11p).

parts.q: What is radio-carbon dating? How to estimate age of ancient objects?
parts.solution:
Radio-carbon dating: A method to determine the age of carbon-containing archaeological or geological samples by measuring the remaining C-14 activity.

Living organisms maintain equilibrium C-14 levels. After death, C-14 decays without replenishment. By comparing the activity of a sample to that of living matter, the age is calculated using:

N = N0e−λt
t = (1/λ) ln(N0/N) = (T1/2/0.693) ln(N0/N)

parts.q: Sample contains 1 × 10<sup>22</sup> C-14 nuclei. What is the activity?
parts.solution:
T1/2 = 5760 years = 5760 × 365.25 × 24 × 3600 s
T1/2 = 1.817 × 1011 s
λ = 0.693/T1/2 = 3.81 × 10−12 s−1

Activity A = λN
A = 3.81 × 10−12 × 1022
A = 3.81 × 1010 Bq
= 3.81 × 1010 / 3.7 × 1010 Ci
A ≈ 1.03 Ci

parts.q:
Modern method of X-ray production.
i) Working principle.
parts.solution: High-speed electrons are accelerated by high voltage and strike a metal target. Their sudden deceleration produces X-rays (bremsstrahlung), and characteristic X-rays are produced when electrons knock out inner-shell electrons.

parts.q: ii) Why metal target of high melting point and high atomic weight?
parts.solution:
High melting point: Only a small fraction of electron energy becomes X-rays; most becomes heat. High melting point prevents the target from melting (e.g., tungsten: 3422°C).

High atomic weight: Heavier atoms have more protons, creating stronger nuclear fields for electron deceleration, producing more intense X-rays with higher energy.

parts.q: iii) How are intensity and quality of X-rays controlled?
parts.solution:
Intensity: Controlled by filament current (heater current). More current means more thermionic emission, more electrons, more X-rays.

Quality (penetrating power): Controlled by accelerating voltage (kV). Higher voltage gives electrons more energy, producing shorter wavelength, more penetrating X-rays.

parts.q: Light λ=400 nm on photosensitive material with work function 2.3 eV. Find maximum KE of photoelectrons.
parts.solution:
E = hc/λ = (6.63×10−34 × 3×108)/(400×10−9)
E = 4.97×10−19 J = 3.10 eV

KEmax = E − φ = 3.10 − 2.30
KEmax = 0.80 eV
= 0.80 × 1.6×10−19 J
= 1.28 × 10−19 J
